column3: Pleuritic LUQ pain with productive cough is a left lower-lobe pneumonia mimicking abdominal pain; a chest X-ray confirms it.
A calcified RUQ cyst in a sheep farmer suggests a hydatid cyst; CT defines the cyst, its daughter cysts and biliary communication.
AF with severe pain out of proportion and bloody stool suggests acute mesenteric ischaemia; angiography (CT or catheter) shows the occlusion.
Recurrent pancreatitis-type pain with near-normal amylase suggests chronic pancreatitis; faecal elastase confirms exocrine insufficiency.
Epigastric pain radiating to the neck with sweating and a soft abdomen may be cardiac; troponin (and ECG) excludes MI.
Large pink confluent warty perianal lesions are condylomata acuminata (HPV); condylomata lata are flat, moist lesions of secondary syphilis.
AF, malar flush and a mid-diastolic murmur indicate mitral stenosis; the enlarged left atrium compresses the oesophagus externally.

A probable CBD stone before cholecystectomy should be cleared first; ERCP confirms and extracts it (MRCP/EUS if the stone is uncertain).

Postprandial RUQ pain lasting 30–60 min is biliary colic from gallstones impacting in the gallbladder neck (Hartmann pouch).
In Mirizzi syndrome a stone in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch compresses the common hepatic duct from outside.
In gallstone pancreatitis ERCP clears stones from the common bile duct.
Chronic RIF pain, diarrhoea and weight loss in a young man suggest ileocaecal Crohn disease; colonoscopy with ileal intubation and biopsy confirms it.
Iron-deficiency anaemia with a RIF mass in a frail, high-risk patient: CT colonography is a safe, less invasive way to assess the colon.
Melaena with tachycardia is an upper GI bleed; OGD identifies and treats the source (with gastric biopsy as needed).

NSAID use, back pain and a major bleed suggest a posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery.
Progressive dysphagia worse for liquids with nocturnal cough is achalasia: failure of relaxation of the distal oesophagus.
H. pylori lives beneath the mucus of the pre-pyloric antrum, so biopsies for the urease test are taken there.
Positive tTG suggests coeliac disease; confirmation needs multiple biopsies from the second part of the duodenum (villous atrophy).
Haematemesis after forceful vomiting is a Mallory–Weiss tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction.
A T2 N0 carcinoma of the gastric body is curable by radical resection; a body tumour needs total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy.
Pancreatic head cancer encasing the SMA/SMV is unresectable; palliate obstruction with a gastrojejunal (± biliary) bypass or stents.
The small bowel (including Meckel diverticulum) is the commonest site of neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumours, often found incidentally.
Postprandial retrosternal burning worse lying down, with odynophagia, is gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (consider OGD for dysphagia).
Free subdiaphragmatic gas on an erect chest X-ray with generalised tenderness indicates a perforated viscus.
Loin-to-groin colicky pain with minimal abdominal signs is renal colic.
Severe upper abdominal pain with amylase > 3× normal is diagnostic of acute pancreatitis.
Tearing chest pain radiating to the back with a widened mediastinum is aortic dissection.
Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting after a holiday of heavy drinking is acute pancreatitis.
Vomiting, absolute constipation, distension and high-pitched (tinkling) bowel sounds indicate small bowel obstruction.
NSAID use followed by a rigid, silent abdomen is a perforated peptic ulcer.
Fever, rigors and loin pain radiating to the groin in a young woman is acute pyelonephritis.
RIF pain progressing rapidly to a tense, generalised peritonitic abdomen in a child is a perforated appendix.
Altered bowel habit with blood mixed in the stool in a 60-year-old is colorectal (colonic) carcinoma until proven otherwise.
Long-standing dyspepsia with melaena and light-headedness is a bleeding duodenal ulcer.
Painless fresh blood on the paper after childbirth is typical of haemorrhoids.
Haematemesis after a bout of vomiting during celebrations is a Mallory–Weiss tear.
Cystic fibrosis can cause biliary cirrhosis and portal hypertension; profuse fresh haematemesis is from oesophageal varices.
In a Richter hernia only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate and perforate without complete obstruction.
A newborn with bowel in the left chest has a congenital (Bochdalek) diaphragmatic hernia.
A Spigelian hernia passes through the linea semilunaris at the lateral rectus border and is often only confirmed by ultrasound.
A pantaloon hernia has direct and indirect sacs straddling the inferior epigastric vessels.
A groin lump protruding straight forward and not controlled by deep-ring pressure is a direct inguinal hernia.
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome: a gastrinoma drives acid hypersecretion and severe, multiple or atypical ulcers.
Adenocarcinoma of the lower third of the oesophagus arises from Barrett metaplasia after long-standing reflux.
Achalasia gives a smooth "bird's beak / rat tail" narrowing at the lower oesophageal sphincter on barium swallow.
Epigastric pain at night relieved by food is typical of duodenal ulcer.
Plummer–Vinson syndrome: iron-deficiency anaemia with dysphagia from a post-cricoid web.
Vomiting with redcurrant-jelly stool in a child is intussusception.
A bluish, tender perianal lump after straining is a perianal haematoma.
Angiodysplasia affects the right colon; colonoscopy shows dilated tortuous vessels and cherry-red spots.
Crohn disease can affect any part of the gut, with deep fissuring ulcers giving a cobblestone mucosa.
Left-sided pain with dark red bleeding and "thumbprinting" (thickened folds) in an older patient is ischaemic colitis.
Recurrent RUQ pain radiating to the scapula without fever is biliary colic.
Cholangiocarcinoma presents with painless jaundice and is a recognised complication of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
RUQ tenderness and guarding with fever and Boas sign (hyperaesthesia below the right scapula) is acute cholecystitis.
Pain, fever and jaundice (Charcot triad) from E. coli infection of an obstructed duct is ascending cholangitis.
Cirrhosis with ascites and anorexia suggests hepatoma (hepatocellular carcinoma).
A pelvic appendix can cause dysuria and diarrhoea; fever, anorexia and RIF tenderness point to acute appendicitis.
Bloody mucoid diarrhoea with weight loss and back pain (sacroiliitis/ankylosing spondylitis) suggests ulcerative colitis.
Sudden pain radiating to the groin and testis with haematuria is a ureteric stone (renal colic), not torsion.
Rectal bleeding at 35 with a father dead of colorectal cancer at 46 suggests familial adenomatous polyposis.
LIF pain with a large bright-red bleed and altered bowel habit in an older woman is acute diverticulitis/diverticular bleeding.
A long-standing hernia that no longer reduces but has no obstruction is incarcerated; it needs urgent repair.
A reducible bulge at a laparoscopic port site is an incisional (port-site) hernia.
An elderly thin woman with obstruction and no visible lump suggests an obturator hernia (gas shadow in the obturator foramen).
A reducible lump above the inguinal ligament with a cough impulse and a family history is an inguinal hernia.
An everted umbilicus that worsens after pregnancy is an umbilical (paraumbilical) hernia.
Sudden collapse with peritonitis on a background of LIF pain is perforated sigmoid diverticular disease.
Fever, upper abdominal tenderness and a positive Murphy sign is acute cholecystitis.
A pelvic appendix may cause urinary symptoms; RIF and suprapubic guarding with fever indicate acute appendicitis.
Progressive constipation, colicky pain, no flatus and a tympanitic distended abdomen is large bowel obstruction.
Epigastric pain to the back after a binge with hypoxia (early ARDS) and a normal erect CXR is acute pancreatitis.
Faeculent vomiting, weight loss and a RIF mass indicate obstructing caecal carcinoma.
Small bowel obstruction with pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree) is gallstone ileus.
Colonic dilatation after spinal surgery in an immobile patient is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome).
Obstruction with a firm tender lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is a strangulated femoral hernia.
A grossly distended non-tender abdomen with a large colonic loop in an elderly constipated patient is sigmoid volvulus.
NSAID use with haematemesis and melaena: a posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery.
Recurrent heavy lower GI bleeding in an elderly man with a normal barium enema suggests angiodysplasia.
Anaemia, weight loss, a RIF mass and hepatomegaly (metastases) indicate caecal carcinoma.
Melaena in an alcoholic with splenomegaly, drowsiness and hypotension is bleeding oesophageal varices.
Microcytic anaemia, change in habit and LIF peritonism with fever suggest a perforated/obstructing sigmoid carcinoma.
Hunger pain that wakes him at night, relieved by food, with weight gain is duodenal ulcer disease.
Progressive dysphagia in a young person with recurrent chest infections (aspiration) is achalasia.
Recurrent ulcer pain then vomiting, dehydration and a succussion splash is gastric outlet (pyloric) stenosis.
Long-standing reflux followed by rapidly progressive dysphagia and weight loss is oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
Haematemesis after repeated vomiting during heavy drinking is a Mallory–Weiss tear.
Flatulent dyspepsia, fatty-food intolerance and RUQ pain suggest gallstones: abdominal ultrasound first.
Endoscopic ultrasound gives the best local T and N staging of oesophageal cancer.
Pancreatic cancer is staged by contrast CT (pancreatic protocol) for vascular involvement and metastases.
Cervical dysphagia, a soft neck swelling and aspiration suggest a pharyngeal pouch: barium swallow (not blind endoscopy).
Staging laparoscopy detects peritoneal seedlings missed by CT before gastric cancer resection.
Fatigue (anaemia), subacute obstruction and a RIF mass in an older woman is caecal carcinoma.
Change in habit with distension and an irregular LIF mass is sigmoid carcinoma.
A young woman with weight loss, fever and a tender RIF mass suggests an inflammatory Crohn mass.
A smooth non-tender RUQ mass after biliary colic is a mucocoele (stone impacted in Hartmann pouch).
A suprapubic mass with menorrhagia-related anaemia in a 45-year-old woman is uterine fibroids.
An irreducible tender lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle with obstruction is a strangulated femoral hernia.
A lump with cough impulse that reduces above and medial to the pubic tubercle is an inguinal hernia.
A hard irregular groin node after a calf melanoma is malignant (metastatic) lymphadenopathy.
A pulsatile groin lump after femoral puncture is a false (pseudo-) aneurysm.
Mucous diarrhoea with hypokalaemia is classic for a secretory rectal villous adenoma.
A painful indurated perianal ulcer in a woman with CIN (HPV) is anal carcinoma.
Constipation with fresh blood on clothes in a child is most often an anal fissure.
Profuse painless dark red bleeding in a fit elderly man suggests angiodysplasia (or diverticular bleeding).
